messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luis, a 25-year-old data scientist of Latin American descent, has been grappling with a heavy weight of distress since his younger brother’s life-threatening illness. At the time, Luis had been just a teenager, but the harrowing experience of watching his brother endure painful treatments and near-death moments left an indelible mark on his psyche. The memory remains vivid yet fragmented; he struggles to piece together the chaotic moments in the hospital — the beeping machines, the sterile scent of antiseptic, and the piercing sound of sirens that seemed to follow him everywhere. Every time he hears a siren, a jolt of fear courses through him, sending him spiraling back to that helpless time. This auditory trigger sends him into a panic, causing him to suppress any anger he feels, fearing that allowing himself to feel even a hint of that emotion would be a betrayal to his brother’s struggle. In the years since that traumatic episode, Luis has developed a repertoire of maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming waves of fear and anxiety that threaten to engulf him. These intrusive thoughts amplify his sense of threat, making it feel as though danger lurks just beyond his awareness, which in turn heightens his sensitivity to any reminders of the trauma. This perceived threat of emotional vulnerability drives him to adopt further avoidance strategies, as he believes that staying stoic is the only way to protect himself from the pain of confronting his feelings. These fragmented memories create a persistent sense of threat, where even the most innocuous sounds can become triggers, reinforcing his anxiety and making him feel perpetually on edge. He avoids hospitals and any medical cues like the plague, steering clear of the very places that remind him of his brother's suffering. Even the faint smell of sweat or body odor can trigger memories he desperately tries to suppress. When these memories surface, the anxiety they invoke leads Luis to avoid places where he might encounter such smells, reinforcing his maladaptive strategy of steering clear of reminders of his brother's suffering. He has come to believe that if he can just avoid these reminders, he can keep the memories at bay. Yet, this avoidance only serves to tighten the grip of his anxiety; when he cannot escape the triggers, he finds himself startled by ordinary sounds that elicit a physical response he cannot control. His heart races and his palms sweat, as if he is back in that moment of terror, perpetually on high alert. This heightened state of vigilance leads him to engage in avoidance behaviors, as he feels that limiting his exposure to potentially triggering situations is the only way to manage the overwhelming threat he perceives. When Luis recalls that traumatic time, he feels as if the memory is a surreal nightmare, almost too extreme to believe it was real. The sequence of events is jumbled in his mind, each recollection bringing forth a wave of terror that he struggles to contain. He often finds himself lying awake at night, unable to sleep, needing to stay vigilant against the intrusive thoughts of his brother’s illness. The physical reactivity is inescapable; he can feel the tension in his muscles and the pounding in his chest whenever he is reminded of the hospital visits. Each trigger reinforces the memory, and the memories further exacerbate his triggers, creating a cycle that feels inescapable. Luis's efforts to suppress his thoughts only seem to amplify his distress. When he tries to push away the memories, they come back stronger, often leaving him in tears. He fears that expressing his feelings will expose him to a vulnerability he cannot afford, so he remains stoic, trapped in a façade of control. This suppression, however, leaves him feeling isolated and disconnected, as if he is living behind a glass wall. As he continues to avoid confronting his memories, they remain vividly intact, making it increasingly difficult for him to break free from the cycle of distress they perpetuate. The more he avoids his feelings and the memories associated with them, the more powerful they become, and the more he finds himself startled by the world around him. At work, the stress has begun to seep into his daily life. Luis has noticed that he struggles to focus, often haunted by the echoes of his past. The constant anxiety and avoidance have created a feedback loop, where his inability to confront his memories heightens his feelings of threat, making even mundane tasks feel overwhelming. The sirens of ambulances outside his office send him spiraling into a state of distress, making it difficult to concentrate on his data analysis. His colleagues have started to notice his withdrawal, and he fears that they see him as less capable or even fragile. This fear amplifies his avoidance, as he believes that distancing himself from his workplace interactions is the only way to protect himself from potential judgment, further entrenching his sense of threat and isolation. This fear only deepens his avoidance; he chooses to work from home, isolating himself further from the very interactions he once enjoyed. After years of battling these overwhelming feelings alone, Luis has finally reached a breaking point. The weight of his avoidance strategies has only deepened his sense of threat, making it feel as though he is trapped in an unending cycle of fear and distress that he can no longer manage alone. The exhaustion from constantly suppressing his trauma has become unbearable. He feels trapped in a life that seems dictated by fear and memories that refuse to fade. Seeking help feels daunting, but he knows he cannot continue this way. What frightens him most is the possibility that he may never be free from the shadows of his past, yet there’s a flicker of hope that perhaps, with the right support, he might find a way to reclaim his life.

violation_explanations: The relationship between triggers and maladaptive strategies is not established; although triggers are mentioned, the text does not clearly indicate that triggers lead to the development of maladaptive strategies.
The text does not show that memory leads to triggers; while memories trigger distress, the causal direction is not clearly stated in the text.
The vignette does not connect maladaptive strategies to memory; it describes avoidance behaviors but does not indicate that these behaviors influence or modify the memories themselves.

There is no clear causal relationship shown between maladaptive strategies and threat; while both are mentioned, the text does not convey that employing maladaptive strategies leads to or increases a sense of threat.
